title: Xenosensors in the gut–liver Axis: from microbiome metabolites to toxic response variability
content:
Abstract
The gut–liver axis is a complex, bidirectional communication network in which metabolites produced by the gut microbiota play an important role in regulating liver function and xenobiotic metabolism. At the center of this interaction is a group of molecular sensors called xenosensors, which include ligand-activated nuclear transcription factors, such as pregnane X receptor (PXR), constitutive androstane receptor (CAR), aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), and farnesoid X receptor (FXR), as well as membrane receptors such as TGR5. By recognizing and responding to endogenous and exogenous chemical compounds, these receptors regulate the expression of enzymes and transporters involved in the metabolism of drugs and other xenobiotics, thereby influencing the body’s detoxification capacity and susceptibility to chemical toxicity. Evidence suggests that gut microbiota-derived metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, and tryptophan derivatives, can directly or indirectly modulate the activity of xenosensors. These findings suggest an important mechanistic link between gut microbiota composition and host toxicological responses. Furthermore, individual differences in the expression and signaling pathways of xenosensors, influenced by factors such as genetic polymorphisms, diet, environmental exposures, and microbiome diversity, can contribute to differences in individual responses to drugs and toxicants. This review aims to summarize current findings on the role of gut microbiota-derived metabolites in the regulation of xenosensors in the gut–liver axis and to investigate the impact of these interactions on xenobiotic metabolism and toxicity. In addition, the mechanistic aspects of this process, its potential applications in clinical and translational fields, including the identification of biomarkers and the development of personalized medicine strategies, as well as gaps in current knowledge that could determine the direction of future research, are discussed. A better understanding of the integrated network of microbiome-derived signals and the activation of hepatic xenosensors is of fundamental importance for predicting individual differences in drug response and sensitivity to environmental pollutants and chemicals, and could help design safer therapeutic strategies and improve risk assessment frameworks.
